kernels.definition: In the circular flow of income, money that households earn returns to firms as spending unless it leaks out of the flow as saving, taxes, or spending on imports.

definitionAnchor.quote: money that households earn returns to firms as spending unless it leaks out of the flow as saving, taxes, or spending on imports

facts.text: Leakages are balanced by injections such as investment, government spending, and exports that add spending back into the flow.

facts.text: When total leakages equal total injections, the circular flow is in balance and national income neither rises nor falls.

mcItems.q: A researcher compares school absences in two towns after one town gets a new bus route and the other does not. What makes this comparison credible as a natural experiment?
op: The towns were comparable apart from the bus-route change.
The town with the new route had a larger student population.
The new route was installed after absences were already falling.
The researcher measured absences in only one town.
mcItems.ex: The towns were comparable apart from the bus-route change. That is the condition that lets the observed difference be linked to the route rather than to some preexisting difference between towns. mcItems.q: One county experiences a factory closure while a neighboring county does not, and unemployment rises more in the first county. When can the rise be attributed to the closure rather than to some other cause?
op: Only when the counties were comparable apart from the closure.
Only when unemployment rose in both counties by the same amount.
Only when the first county had more people looking for work before the closure.
Only when the closure happened after the unemployment increase began.
mcItems.ex: Only when the counties were comparable apart from the closure. That comparability is what makes the closure the plausible cause of the larger rise instead of a confounding factor. Same-sized changes, prior labor-market size, or a timing reversal would not establish that link.

keyTerms.df: A study setup that uses an outside change affecting one group but not another to estimate a causal effect from observed data.
keyTerms.eg: A bus-route change in one town but not a similar neighboring town can be used to compare how school absences changed.
keyTerms.mi: It is just any study that uses a survey or dataset.
keyTerms.cx: The correction is that the key feature is an external change that creates a useful comparison, not merely the presence of data.

keyTerms.df: Another influence that can move the outcome and make a causal comparison less trustworthy.
keyTerms.eg: If a storm hits only the county that also loses the factory, the storm is a confounding factor when trying to explain unemployment changes.
keyTerms.mi: It is the policy or event being tested.
keyTerms.cx: The correction is that a confounder is a separate influence that can distort the comparison, not the change under study.

mcItems.q: A local economy has households saving and paying taxes in the same total amount that firms receive from investment, government spending, and exports. What is the result for the circular flow?
op: The flow remains in balance, so national income neither rises nor falls.
The flow expands, so national income rises automatically.
The flow contracts, so national income falls automatically.
The flow becomes unbalanced, so income must change direction.
mcItems.ex: The flow remains in balance when total leakages equal total injections, so national income neither rises nor falls. The tempting mistake is to treat leakages alone as enough to shrink the economy, but the added spending from investment, government spending, and exports offsets them here.

mcItems.q: Households in an economy earn income, save part of it, and pay taxes, while firms, government, and foreign buyers supply extra spending. What must be true if the circular flow is to stay balanced?
op: The added spending must match the spending that leaves the flow.
The added spending must be zero if saving occurs.
Taxes must always be larger than saving for balance.
Exports must equal imports in every case.
mcItems.ex: The added spending must match the spending that leaves the flow because injections balance leakages in the circular flow. A common misconception is that any saving automatically breaks the flow, but balance is preserved when outside spending offsets the spending that leaks out.

keyTerms.df: Money that leaves the spending stream before it reaches firms as current demand.
keyTerms.eg: In class, a household’s decision to save part of its income is treated as a leakage from the circular flow.
keyTerms.mi: A leakage is any payment made by firms to households.
keyTerms.cx: A correction is that leakages are the parts of income that do not return immediately as spending.

keyTerms.df: Spending added back into the flow from outside household consumption.
keyTerms.eg: When the government buys goods, that spending acts as an injection in the circular flow.
keyTerms.mi: An injection is the same thing as saving by households.
keyTerms.cx: A correction is that injections are extra spending that comes back into the flow and helps offset leakages.

mcItems.q: A factory has 100 machines at the start of the year. During the year, the firm buys 12 new machines and retires 5 old ones. What is the change in its equipment stock over the year?
op: An increase of 7 machines
An increase of 12 machines
A decrease of 5 machines
No change in the equipment stock
mcItems.ex: An increase of 7 machines is correct because net investment equals gross investment minus depreciation, so 12 minus 5 gives a 7-machine rise in the capital stock. The tempting mistake is to count only purchases; that ignores the machines lost from depreciation and overstates the stock change.

mcItems.q: Which statement best describes when a capital stock grows?
op: It grows only when net investment is positive
It grows whenever gross investment is positive
It grows whenever depreciation is positive
It grows whenever equipment is replaced
mcItems.ex: It grows only when net investment is positive is correct because the stock rises when additions exceed losses over the period. A common confusion is to focus on gross investment alone, but if depreciation is larger, the stock does not grow.

keyTerms.df: The amount of productive equipment, structures, and tools available at a point in time.
keyTerms.eg: A firm's plant, machines, and tools at the end of March are part of its capital stock.
keyTerms.mi: It means the dollar value of sales during a year.
keyTerms.cx: Use the stock idea to describe what is on hand at a moment, not what is earned over a period.

keyTerms.df: Gross additions minus wear and retirements over a period; it is the period-to-period change in the capital stock.
keyTerms.eg: If a business buys 10 forklifts and loses 4 to depreciation in a year, its net investment is 6 forklifts.
keyTerms.mi: It is the same thing as total spending on new equipment.
keyTerms.cx: Subtract losses from purchases to find the amount that actually changes the stock.

mcItems.q: One county experiences a factory closure while a neighboring county does not, and unemployment rises more in the first county. When can the rise be attributed to the closure rather than to some other cause?
op: Only when the counties were comparable apart from the closure.
Only when unemployment rose in both counties by the same amount.
Only when the first county had more people looking for work before the closure.
Only when the closure happened after the unemployment increase began.
mcItems.ex: Only when the counties were comparable apart from the closure. That comparability is what makes the closure the plausible cause of the larger rise instead of a confounding factor. Same-sized changes, prior labor-market size, or a timing reversal would not establish that link.

A survey asks people about their opinions after a change

mcItems.ex: Policy or external event hits one group, so causal effect can be estimated. The groups must be comparable; random assignment is not required here.

keyTerms.df: A study setup that uses an outside change affecting one group but not another to estimate a causal effect from observed data.
keyTerms.eg: A bus-route change in one town but not a similar neighboring town can be used to compare how school absences changed.
keyTerms.mi: It is just any study that uses a survey or dataset.
keyTerms.cx: The correction is that the key feature is an external change that creates a useful comparison, not merely the presence of data.

keyTerms.df: Another influence that can move the outcome and make a causal comparison less trustworthy.
keyTerms.eg: If a storm hits only the county that also loses the factory, the storm is a confounding factor when trying to explain unemployment changes.
keyTerms.mi: It is the policy or event being tested.
keyTerms.cx: The correction is that a confounder is a separate influence that can distort the comparison, not the change under study.

mcItems.q: A local economy has households saving and paying taxes in the same total amount that firms receive from investment, government spending, and exports. What is the result for the circular flow?
op: The flow remains in balance, so national income neither rises nor falls.
The flow expands, so national income rises automatically.
The flow contracts, so national income falls automatically.
The flow becomes unbalanced, so income must change direction.
mcItems.ex: The flow remains in balance when total leakages equal total injections, so national income neither rises nor falls. The tempting mistake is to treat leakages alone as enough to shrink the economy, but the added spending from investment, government spending, and exports offsets them here.

mcItems.q: Households in an economy earn income, save part of it, and pay taxes, while firms, government, and foreign buyers supply extra spending. What must be true if the circular flow is to stay balanced?
op: The added spending must match the spending that leaves the flow.
The added spending must be zero if saving occurs.
Taxes must always be larger than saving for balance.
Exports must equal imports in every case.
mcItems.ex: The added spending must match the spending that leaves the flow because injections balance leakages in the circular flow. A common misconception is that any saving automatically breaks the flow, but balance is preserved when outside spending offsets the spending that leaks out.

keyTerms.df: Money that leaves the spending stream before it reaches firms as current demand.
keyTerms.eg: In class, a household’s decision to save part of its income is treated as a leakage from the circular flow.
keyTerms.mi: A leakage is any payment made by firms to households.
keyTerms.cx: A correction is that leakages are the parts of income that do not return immediately as spending.

keyTerms.df: Spending added back into the flow from outside household consumption.
keyTerms.eg: When the government buys goods, that spending acts as an injection in the circular flow.
keyTerms.mi: An injection is the same thing as saving by households.
keyTerms.cx: A correction is that injections are extra spending that comes back into the flow and helps offset leakages.

mcItems.q: A factory has 100 machines at the start of the year. During the year, the firm buys 12 new machines and retires 5 old ones. What is the change in its equipment stock over the year?
op: An increase of 7 machines
An increase of 12 machines
A decrease of 5 machines
No change in the equipment stock
mcItems.ex: An increase of 7 machines is correct because net investment equals gross investment minus depreciation, so 12 minus 5 gives a 7-machine rise in the capital stock. The tempting mistake is to count only purchases; that ignores the machines lost from depreciation and overstates the stock change.

mcItems.q: Which statement best describes when a capital stock grows?
op: It grows only when net investment is positive
It grows whenever gross investment is positive
It grows whenever depreciation is positive
It grows whenever equipment is replaced
mcItems.ex: It grows only when net investment is positive is correct because the stock rises when additions exceed losses over the period. A common confusion is to focus on gross investment alone, but if depreciation is larger, the stock does not grow.

keyTerms.df: The amount of productive equipment, structures, and tools available at a point in time.
keyTerms.eg: A firm's plant, machines, and tools at the end of March are part of its capital stock.
keyTerms.mi: It means the dollar value of sales during a year.
keyTerms.cx: Use the stock idea to describe what is on hand at a moment, not what is earned over a period.

keyTerms.df: Gross additions minus wear and retirements over a period; it is the period-to-period change in the capital stock.
keyTerms.eg: If a business buys 10 forklifts and loses 4 to depreciation in a year, its net investment is 6 forklifts.
keyTerms.mi: It is the same thing as total spending on new equipment.
keyTerms.cx: Subtract losses from purchases to find the amount that actually changes the stock.
